newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE's state-backed firms get mixed review.
newsitem.headline: UAE's state-backed firms get mixed review.

text.p: Attempts by the United Arab Emirates to give its private sector a bigger role in the oil-driven economy and reduce government dominance have turned out to be a double-edged sword, analysts said on Tuesday.
A recent spate of state-backed company launches is part of the official effort to involve the private sector more and diversify from oil.
But some say the government's support for firms may be crossing the fine line between encouragement and crowding out.
In the past few months three companies have been launched. The governments and ruling families of the seven emirates in the UAE federation own at least 10 percent in each.

"State shareholding here is looked at in a positive light. It implies some purchases of the company's services by the government, which probably means good revenue for other shareholders in the long run," an Abu Dhabi-based banker said.
"But the government really should be privatising its shareholding, not increasing it horizontally. It should really let the private sector stand alone."
Others say the fact that government has a share in private companies is what makes them attractive to investors.

"It is a good thing that government is involved. It is interested in ensuring the development of the market takes place in a sensible manner. Their role is in encouraging investors," HSBC Financial Services Middle East chief executive Mukhtar Hussain said.
Last month Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank was launched with capital of one billion dirhams ($272 million). Abu Dhabi government will own 10 percent and the president's private office five percent.
The new Oasis International Leasing on Monday offered 55 percent of its shares to the public. Abu Dhabi's government and ruling family will control more than 12 percent.

In March, Emaar Properties was launched with 540 million dirhams capital. Two weeks later, and amid strong investor demand the Dubai government stepped in and instructed Emaar to raise its capital to one billion dirhams. Dubai took 10 percent.
Emaar was five times oversubscribed.

"I find it interesting that to satisfy primarily investor demand, the government increased the Emaar issue. It shows the market is in a process of evolution. Hopefully as rules are promulgated we will see more consistency," said one analyst.
But others said Dubai's participation was cause for concern. "This simply doesn't happen in the real world. The regulatory oversight of these issues should be looked at," said one.

The UAE is the only Gulf state without a formal stock exchange. Amid high domestic liquidity and scant investment opportunities at home, many wealthy UAE nationals put their money into the developed financial markets of the West.
"One of the challenges for Gulf states is to attract back capital domiciled offshore because of the limited investment opportunities at home," said a banker.

Another challenge is to widen the narrow investor base in the 30-odd traded firms. But government involvement in new issues and slow moves towards its stated goal of privatising some utilities may be inhibiting this, analysts say.
"The government is pretty much in everything that is larger than a corner grocery store. This creates a problem for the local investor who has limited investment chances," said one.
Government has a controlling, if not majority, stake in most local banks. "It should privatise things. It can better inspire confidence by being more transparent," said a banker.
($1=3.67 dirhams)
